# Madhupiṇḍika Sutta (MN 18 (PTS MN i 108))

**ID:** MN 18 (PTS MN i 108)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Madhupiṇḍika Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Honey-Cake
**PTS:** MN i 108
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn18
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Madhupiṇḍika Sutta* ("The Honey-Cake" or "The Honeyball Discourse", MN 18) is set at Nigrodha's Park in Kapilavatthu, where the Sakyan Daṇḍapāṇi approaches the Buddha and discourteously asks what the ascetic asserts and proclaims [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Kuan 2008]. The Buddha replies with a concise summary stating that his teaching allows one to live without dispute in the world and without obsessions rooted in perceptions (*saññā*), thereby tracing conflicts, arguments, and afflictions to mental proliferation (*papañca*) [Passi 2006; Kuan 2008; McTighe 2011; SuttaCentral]. When Daṇḍapāṇi leaves dissatisfied and the Buddha retreats to his dwelling, the monks ask Venerable Mahākaccāna to unpack this terse utterance; Mahākaccāna provides a famous step-by-step exposition of sensory contact, perception, and the proliferation of thought [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Klaus & Hartmann 2007]. The Buddha endorses his exposition entirely, noting he would have answered in the exact same manner, which later tradition cited as justification for regarding disciples' expositions as the Buddha's own word (*buddhabhāsita*) [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Norman 1983]. Following Ānanda's simile comparing the teaching to a sweet honey-cake (*madhupiṇḍika*) enjoyed by a starving person, the Buddha adopts this title for the discourse [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Klaus & Hartmann 2007].

Curated parallels include a full discourse in the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* (MĀ 115), as well as *Ekottarika Āgama* 40.10 (EĀ 40.10), *Saṃyuktāgama* 304 (SĀ 304), a Sanskrit fragment (SHT sutta 71), Tibetan *Upāyikā* 3.059, and canonical Pali parallels such as the *Chachakka Sutta* (MN 148) and SN 35.60 [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus confirms extensive cross-linguistic alignment with MĀ 115 and EĀ 40.10, and also highlights matches with Candrakīrti's *Prasannapadā*, which recontextualizes this canonical model of conceptual proliferation and afflictions [DharmaNexus; Walser 1997]. Internally, DharmaNexus shows extensive text reuse with AN 10, SN 35, and especially MN 138 and MN 133, which follow the same structural framework of Mahākaccāna elaborating on the Buddha's brief teachings [DharmaNexus; Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Galasek 2016]. Comparative analysis shows that while Ānanda speaks the honey-cake simile in the Pali version, MĀ 115 attributes the simile to the Buddha, applying its sweetness to the contemplation of any of the six sense bases [Klaus & Hartmann 2007].

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral entry for MN 18 — Provided titles, blurb, and curated parallels across Pali, Chinese, Sanskrit, and Tibetan corpora.

- [Kuan 2008] Tse-fu Kuan, Mindfulness in Early Buddhism — Discussed the Buddha's initial reply to Daṇḍapāṇi on perception and bhavābhava with reference to Chinese parallels.
- [Walser 1997] Joseph Gaither Walser, Logic, Scripture and Allusion: Recontextualization of Canon in Early Mādhyamika of Nāgārjuna (Akutobhayā) (1997) — Noted the Chinese parallel and Candrakīrti's shared perspective on conceptual proliferation and afflictions.
